title: Constituent structure and constituency tests
summary: From zero: what a constituent is, the three tests that prove one (substitution, movement, fragment answer) with each term defined before it's used, how to use the tests to pull apart an ambiguous sentence, and how to write a full Quiz 2 answer.
sourceNote: Week 5 handout (Constituent structure), TrevTutor 'Constituents and Constituency Tests', the Sep 15 and 17 classes. Quiz 2 covers this. Rebuilt for readers who missed class: pro-form, topicalization, cleft, N-bar and finiteness are each defined before they are used.

sections.heading: Start here: what a constituent is

blocks.body: A group of words that **behaves as one unit** in a sentence. You can't see it by looking; you prove it with a **test**. A single word always counts; the tests are for strings of two or more words.

blocks.md: **One example.** In *Those tall spies in the garden will quickly stash the evidence after midnight*, is *the evidence* a unit? Replace it with *it*: …will quickly stash **it** after midnight. Works. So yes. Is *stash the* a unit? Replace it with any one word: nothing works. So no. Every pair of neighbors **looks** like a group; only the tests tell you which ones are real.

cards.title: Substitution
lines: Swap the string for one short word.
*the evidence* → *it*

cards.title: Movement
lines: Move the string somewhere else.
*The evidence, they stashed.*

cards.title: Fragment answer
lines: Let it answer a question by itself.
*What did they stash? The evidence.*

blocks.caption: The three tests. Passing any one of them proves the string is a constituent.

rows.label: Can you then say 'not a constituent'?

blocks.caption: The rule Dr. Nie stresses: a pass is proof, a fail is silence. Some real constituents fail one test and pass another.

Every node is a claim that those words form a unit, and substitution ('they', 'it', 'then', 'do so'), movement, and fragment answers are how you defend each claim. blocks.prompt: *The dog chased the cat.* Is *chased the* a constituent? Try one test.
blocks.answer: No. Substitution: no single word replaces *chased the* (*The dog **it** cat* is nonsense). Movement and fragment answers fail too.

sections.heading: Test 1: substitution (swap it for one word)

blocks.body: A short word that stands in for a whole unit. *It*, *they*, *him* stand in for a noun phrase; *there*, *then* for a place or time phrase; *do so* for a verb phrase. 'Pro' means 'in place of', like pronoun.
Replace the string with one pro-form. If the sentence still works (and means the same thing), the string is a constituent. The pro-form also tells you what **kind** of phrase it is.

rows: she, he, they, them, it, something
N (N-bar: noun + its dependents, minus D)
those tall [spies in the garden] → those tall ones
will [stash the evidence] → will do so
blocks.slide: Which pro-form goes with which phrase

blocks.body: A middle-sized unit: the noun **plus** what's attached to it, **minus** the determiner. In *those tall spies in the garden*, the N-bar is *tall spies in the garden*. Its pro-form is *one(s)*: those **ones**. It shows that a noun phrase has a layer inside it.

lines: Those tall spies in the garden will quickly stash the evidence after midnight.
[Those tall spies in the garden] → They will quickly stash the evidence after midnight.  ✓ NP
those tall [spies in the garden] → those tall ones  ✓ N-bar
[in the garden] → there  ✓ PP
will [quickly stash the evidence after midnight] → will do so  ✓ VP
[the evidence] → it  ✓ NP
[after midnight] → then  ✓ PP
[spies in] → ???  ✗   [stash the] → ???  ✗   [evidence after] → ???  ✗

blocks.body: **'ones' never takes the determiner.** Those tall **ones** works; '*ones in the garden' for the whole phrase does not. That's why NP (with *the*/*those*) and N-bar (without) are two different units.

blocks.prompt: *She met the new teacher from Ohio.* Replace *teacher from Ohio* with one word. What does that prove?
blocks.answer: She met the new **one**. One word replaced *teacher from Ohio*, so it's a unit: an N-bar. *the* stays outside, as always.

sections.heading: Test 2: movement (can it travel as a block?)

blocks.body: Pick up the string and put it somewhere else in the sentence. If the result is grammatical, the words traveled together, so they're one unit. English has two easy ways to move things: topicalization and clefting.
Move the string to the **front**, followed by a comma: *The evidence, the spies will stash after midnight.* It sounds a bit dramatic, but it's grammatical.
Put the string in the frame **It's ___ that…**: *It's the evidence that the spies will stash.* 'Cleft' means split: the sentence is split around the string.

lines: Those tall spies in the garden will quickly stash the evidence after midnight.
frames.caption: Test 2 is movement: pick up a string and put it somewhere else. If the sentence still works, the string moved as one block.

lines: Those tall spies in the garden will quickly stash the evidence after midnight.
The evidence, those tall spies will quickly stash after midnight.  ✓
frames.caption: Topicalization: move 'the evidence' to the front. Works, so 'the evidence' is a unit.

lines: Those tall spies in the garden will quickly stash the evidence after midnight.
The evidence, those tall spies will quickly stash after midnight.  ✓
After midnight, those tall spies will quickly stash the evidence.  ✓
frames.caption: Front 'after midnight'. Works too.

lines: Those tall spies in the garden will quickly stash the evidence after midnight.
It's the evidence that those tall spies will quickly stash after midnight.  ✓
frames.caption: Clefting: wrap it in 'It's ___ that…'. 'the evidence' fits the slot, so it's a unit.

lines: Those tall spies in the garden will quickly stash the evidence after midnight.
*Stash the, those tall spies will quickly evidence after midnight.  ✗
frames.caption: Now a fake unit: 'stash the'. It can't move. Every piece of evidence says it's not a constituent.

blocks.md: **A failed movement test proves nothing** Handout: 'Some constituents are too deeply embedded within other constituents to undergo movement.' '*The garden, those tall spies in will stash the evidence' fails: but 'the garden' IS a constituent (substitution: 'in it'). ==Movement can only give you a yes.== If it says no, try another test before concluding anything.

blocks.prompt: Use a cleft to prove *after midnight* is a constituent.
blocks.answer: *It's after midnight that those tall spies will stash the evidence.* ✓

sections.heading: Test 3: fragment answer (can it answer alone?)

blocks.body: Ask a question about the sentence (who, what, where, when, what did they do). If the string can be the **whole answer**, said on its own, it's a constituent. Only units can stand alone like that.

lines: Those tall spies in the garden will quickly stash the evidence after midnight.
frames.caption: Test 3 is the fragment answer: ask a question about the sentence. If the string can be the whole answer by itself, it's a unit.

lines: Those tall spies in the garden will quickly stash the evidence after midnight.
Q: Who will stash the evidence?
A: Those tall spies in the garden.  ✓
frames.caption: The whole subject answers 'who?'. NP constituent.

lines: Those tall spies in the garden will quickly stash the evidence after midnight.
Q: Where are the spies?
A: In the garden.  ✓
frames.caption: 'where?' is answered by the PP.

lines: Those tall spies in the garden will quickly stash the evidence after midnight.
Q: What will they do?
A: Quickly stash the evidence after midnight.  ✓
frames.caption: 'what will they do?' is answered by a whole VP.

lines: Those tall spies in the garden will quickly stash the evidence after midnight.
A: *Stash the.  ✗
frames.caption: No question in English has 'stash the' as its answer. Not a unit.

blocks.title: Question → fragment
blocks.body:
Those tall spies in the garden will quickly stash the evidence after midnight.

1. Who will stash the evidence?: 'Those tall spies in the garden.' ✓ NP
2. Where are the spies?: 'In the garden.' ✓ PP
3. What will they stash?: 'The evidence.' ✓ NP
4. When?: 'After midnight.' ✓ PP
5. What will they do?: 'Quickly stash the evidence after midnight.' ✓ VP (and 'Stash the evidence after midnight.' ✓: the smaller VP)
6. *'Stash the.': no question has that answer. ✗
blocks.slide: All the fragment answers for handout (3)

blocks.prompt: *Mia left her keys on the counter.* Prove *on the counter* is a constituent with a fragment answer.
blocks.answer: *Where did Mia leave her keys?* *On the counter.* ✓

sections.heading: Using the tests on an ambiguous sentence

blocks.body: One word order, **two groupings**, two meanings. The words aren't ambiguous; the structure is. The tests let you prove each grouping exists.

blocks.md: 'The thief tripped that unlucky man with a cane.' Two meanings: the thief used a cane, or the man carries a cane. Chapter 0 showed these as two trees. Now you can *prove* both trees exist with tests: ==each reading passes a test the other fails==.

blocks.slide: Two trees, and the tests that tell them apart

blocks.title: 'with a cane' attaches to the verb
blocks.body:
Show 'with a cane' is a separate constituent from the NP.

1. Cleft: 'It's with a cane that the thief tripped that unlucky man.' ✓: the PP moved away from 'man', so it wasn't inside the NP.
2. Substitution: 'The thief tripped him with a cane.' ✓: 'him' replaces 'that unlucky man' and leaves 'with a cane' behind.
3. Do-so: 'The thief tripped that unlucky man with a cane, and the burglar did so with a rope.' ✓: 'did so' = 'tripped that unlucky man', and the instrument is outside it.
blocks.slide: Reading A: the cane is the instrument

blocks.title: 'with a cane' attaches to the noun
blocks.body:
Show 'that unlucky man with a cane' is one NP.

1. Substitution: 'The thief tripped him.' ✓ where 'him' = 'that unlucky man with a cane': the whole thing, cane included.
2. Fragment: 'Who did the thief trip?': 'That unlucky man with a cane.' ✓
3. Topicalization: 'That unlucky man with a cane, the thief tripped.' ✓: the PP moved along with the NP, so it's inside it.
blocks.answer: Same string, two constituent structures. Each test result is evidence for one of them.
blocks.slide: Reading B: the man has the cane

blocks.md: **Where you'll meet this after the exam** PP-attachment is the ambiguity that runs the world's worst headlines: editors call them ==crash blossoms==, after the real headline 'Violinist linked to JAL crash blossoms': and the lurch you feel reading one is you attaching a constituent early, then re-parsing. It's a live NLP benchmark: parsers still misattach PPs, which is why a photo search for 'man with telescope' returns both readings. And it's a genuine legal problem: contract disputes turn on whether a trailing modifier ('…within 30 days') attaches to the last item or the whole list, and courts run named canons (the 'last-antecedent rule') that are constituency claims in robes. The tests you just ran on the cane sentence are how you'd brief that argument.

sections.heading: A note on tense: finite vs non-finite verb phrases

blocks.body: A verb is **finite** when it carries tense itself (*submitted*, *submits*). It's **non-finite** when it doesn't, usually because a helper like *will* carries the tense instead (*will **submit***).

blocks.md: 'Farah **will submit** the assignment': the VP after the modal is **non-finite** (no tense on 'submit'). Substitution: 'Farah will do so.' ✓ Fragment: 'What will Farah do?: Submit the assignment.' ✓ Clean.
blocks.slide: Finite vs non-finite VPs behave differently

blocks.md: 'Farah **submitted** the assignment': the VP is **finite** (tense is on the verb). Substitution needs do-support to carry the tense: 'Farah did so.' ✓ Fragment answer: 'What did Farah do?: *Submitted the assignment' is marginal; the natural fragment is 'Submit the assignment', with the tense stripped. Her point: ==some tests interact with tense==, so say which kind of VP you're testing.

sections.heading: Practice: a full Quiz 2 answer (handout (4) to (6))

blocks.md: **What she asks** 'Identify all syntactic categories. Identify constituents in each sentence, using each type of constituency test (substitution, movement, fragment answer) at least once.' So a full answer = ==labels + at least three constituents, each with a named test and the actual test sentence written out==.

blocks.caption: Quiz 2's inner loop. Run the tests in this order: substitution is quickest, movement is the flashiest evidence, fragment answers rescue strings the others miss. Land in the green box once and you're done: write the actual test sentence, name the test, move on. The amber box is the graded subtlety: a failed test is silence, not a 'no': only a string that fails everything while straddling two phrases gets declared a non-constituent. Hover any step.
blocks.slide: The test loop: substitute → move → fragment

blocks.title: That officer from the precinct sauntered away very slowly.
blocks.body:
Categories, then three constituents with three different tests.

1. Categories: That D · officer N · from P · the D · precinct N · sauntered V · away Adv (particle) · very Adv · slowly Adv.
2. Substitution: [That officer from the precinct] → 'He sauntered away very slowly.' ✓ NP.
3. Movement (cleft): [very slowly] → 'It was very slowly that that officer sauntered away.' ✓ AdvP.
4. Fragment: 'What did the officer do?': [Sauntered away very slowly.] ✓ VP.
5. Bonus: [from the precinct] → 'It's from the precinct that the officer is' / fragment 'From where?': 'From the precinct.' ✓ PP.

blocks.title: I will invest in some cryptocurrency to fund my globe-trotting lifestyle.
blocks.body:
Three constituents, three tests.

1. Categories: I N · will Mod · invest V · in P · some D · cryptocurrency N · to T · fund V · my D · globe-trotting Adj · lifestyle N.
2. Substitution (do so): 'I will [do so] to fund my lifestyle.' ✓ → 'invest in some cryptocurrency' is a VP.
3. Movement (cleft): 'It's to fund my globe-trotting lifestyle that I will invest in some cryptocurrency.' ✓ → the purpose clause is a constituent (an adjunct).
4. Fragment: 'In what will you invest?': 'In some cryptocurrency.' ✓ PP.
5. Substitution: [my globe-trotting lifestyle] → 'to fund it' ✓ NP.

blocks.title: Lee paraded his favorite new motorbikes around town.
blocks.body:
Is 'motorbikes around town' a constituent?

1. Try substitution: 'them' replaces 'his favorite new motorbikes': 'Lee paraded them around town' ✓: but that leaves 'around town' outside. No pro-form covers 'motorbikes around town' alone.
2. Try movement: '*Motorbikes around town, Lee paraded his favorite new.' ✗
3. Try fragment: 'What did Lee parade?': 'His favorite new motorbikes.' ✓: the answer stops before 'around town'. '*Motorbikes around town' is not an answer to any question.
4. Conclusion: 'motorbikes around town' is NOT a constituent. 'around town' is a PP adjunct of the verb ('It's around town that Lee paraded them' ✓), sister to the object NP, not inside it. Compare reading A of the cane sentence.

blocks.prompt: 'The spies hid in the garden.' Prove 'in the garden' is a constituent three ways.
blocks.answer: Substitution: 'The spies hid there.' Cleft: 'It's in the garden that the spies hid.' Fragment: 'Where did the spies hide?': 'In the garden.'

No. No pro-form ('*The spies did-so the garden'), can't move ('*Hid in, the spies the garden'), can't answer a question. The verb and the preposition belong to different phrases: 'in' heads the PP 'in the garden', which is a dependent of 'hid'.

blocks.term: The three tests, in one line each
blocks.body: **Substitution**: replace the string with one pro-form (pronoun / one(s) / do so / there, then). **Movement**: topicalize it or cleft it ('It's X that…'). **Fragment answer**: let it answer a wh-question alone. Pass any one → constituent. Fail one → try another.

rows: A group of words that behaves as one unit; proven by a test.
A short word standing in for a unit: it, they, there, then, do so, one(s).
Test 1: swap the string for one pro-form.
Move the string to the front: The evidence, they stashed.
Test 3: the string answers a question by itself.
A noun plus its attachments, without the determiner; replaced by one(s).
One word order, two groupings, two meanings.
The verb carries tense itself / a helper like 'will' carries it.
blocks.title: Words from this chapter

exercises.title: Prove a constituent three ways
exercises.prompt: 'The children found a wallet under the old bridge.' Prove that *under the old bridge* is a constituent using all three tests, writing out the actual test sentence for each. Then show that *a wallet under* is NOT one.
hints: Substitution: find one pro-form that replaces the whole string ('there' for places). Movement: front it, or cleft it ('It was ___ that…'). Fragment: ask a question the string alone can answer.
The mistake is describing the tests instead of running them. Write the real sentence and mark it ✓ or *. A test you didn't write out isn't evidence.
For the non-constituent, show at least one test *failing* with an asterisked sentence. One clean failure is enough, but showing two is stronger.
solution: Movement (fronting): '*Under the old bridge*, the children found a wallet.' ✓ Cleft: 'It was under the old bridge that the children found a wallet.' ✓
Fragment: 'Where did the children find a wallet?': 'Under the old bridge.' ✓

*a wallet under*: no pro-form replaces it ('✱The children found it the old bridge'); can't move ('✱A wallet under, the children found the old bridge'); can't answer a question. Not a constituent: it straddles the NP and the PP.
exercises.why: Constituency tests are how syntacticians settle arguments without appealing to intuition alone, and they're the reasoning behind every bracket in a treebank. They're also the oral exam's core: the examiner wants to see you *run* the test, not name it.

exercises.title: Pull apart a structural ambiguity
exercises.prompt: 'She watched the man with the binoculars.' Give the two meanings, then use one constituency test to show which structure each meaning has: a test that succeeds under one reading and fails under the other.
hints: Meaning 1: she used the binoculars. Meaning 2: the man had them. The question is whether 'with the binoculars' groups with 'the man' (inside the NP) or with 'watched' (a separate phrase in the VP).

The error is picking a test that gives the same result for both readings. Substitution of the NP with a pronoun is the sharp one: if 'him' replaces 'the man with the binoculars', the PP was inside the NP.
Try: 'She watched him.' Under which reading does 'him' still mean 'the man with the binoculars'? Then try fronting the PP: 'With the binoculars, she watched the man': which reading survives?
solution: Reading A (instrument): she used binoculars to watch. Reading B (modifier): the man who had binoculars.
Pronoun substitution: 'She watched him' can mean B ('him' = the man with the binoculars): so under B, [the man with the binoculars] is one NP constituent. Under A the PP isn't part of 'him'.
PP fronting: 'With the binoculars, she watched the man' has only reading A: so under A, [with the binoculars] is a separate VP-level constituent that can move; under B it's stuck inside the NP.
Two structures: A = watched [the man] [with the binoculars]; B = watched [the man [with the binoculars]].
exercises.why: PP-attachment ambiguity is the single most common structural ambiguity in English and one of the hardest problems in parsing: every NLP system gets some of these wrong. Knowing how the tests separate the readings is how you'd debug one, and it's the same argument that settles what a trailing modifier attaches to in a contract clause.

exercises.title: Pick the pro-form
exercises.prompt: Which pro-form tests whether *in the kitchen* is a constituent in *We ate in the kitchen*?
hints: Read each option out loud and cross off the ones that are clearly wrong.
The chapter's cards in this section have the exact fact you need.
Pick the one that matches the definition word for word.
exercises.why: Choosing the right pro-form also tells you the phrase type.

choices.feedback: Yes: a place phrase (PP) is replaced by 'there'.

exercises.title: What does a failed test mean?
exercises.prompt: *The garden* fails the movement test in *Those spies in the garden will stash it* ('*The garden, those spies in will stash it'). What can you conclude?
hints: Read each option out loud and cross off the ones that are clearly wrong.
The chapter's cards in this section have the exact fact you need.
Pick the one that matches the definition word for word.
solution: **Nothing yet.** Try substitution: the spies in **it**. ✓ So it is a constituent.
exercises.why: Dr. Nie: 'you may need to try multiple tests before you find one that works'.

choices.feedback: Right. A fail is silence. Substitution ('in it') shows it IS a constituent.
One failed test never proves that; it's too deeply embedded to move.

exercises.title: Which cleft works?
exercises.prompt: Which cleft proves a constituent in *Ana bought a red bike yesterday*?
hints: Read each option out loud and cross off the ones that are clearly wrong.
The chapter's cards in this section have the exact fact you need.
Pick the one that matches the definition word for word.
solution: **It was a red bike that Ana bought yesterday.**
exercises.why: Writing out the actual test sentence is what earns the points on Quiz 2.

choices.text: It was a red bike that Ana bought yesterday.
choices.feedback: Yes: 'a red bike' fits the slot, so it's a unit.

choices.text: It was bought a that Ana red bike yesterday.
It was Ana bought that a red bike yesterday.
choices.feedback: The frame is broken: 'Ana bought' isn't what goes in the slot here.

choices.text: It was red bike yesterday that Ana bought a.

exercises.title: Which question?
exercises.prompt: To prove *to her sister* is a constituent in *Jo sent a card to her sister*, which question do you ask?
hints: Read each option out loud and cross off the ones that are clearly wrong.
The chapter's cards in this section have the exact fact you need.
Pick the one that matches the definition word for word.
solution: **Who did Jo send a card to?** → *To her sister.* ✓
exercises.why: Pick the question whose natural answer is exactly the string.

choices.text: Who did Jo send a card to?
choices.feedback: Yes: the answer 'To her sister.' stands alone.
That question is answered by 'a card'.
A yes/no question is answered by yes or no, not a fragment.
That asks about time, which isn't in the sentence.
